Satisfying a constraint more closely need not make the generated distribution more accurate. We therefore compare penalised and unpenalised generative modelling through their expected squared $2$-Wasserstein error. Our analysis covers both vector-valued and functional data in a Hilbert-space setting. We first derive geometric criteria that account for constraint violations and the distribution of samples after projection onto the constraint set. We then solve the statistical comparison explicitly for specific velocity-field classes and constraints via flow matching. In this model, penalisation improves accuracy exactly when the reduction in estimation variance outweighs the increase in squared bias. The resulting formula shows how this trade-off depends on sample size, the model class, the noise schedule, and the penalty weight.

2610.15690-7348482c59bb.title: Notes on Uniform Policy Score Bounds and Lipschitz Continuity for Truncated Gaussian, Product Cauchy, Boltzmann, and Softmax Policies
2610.15690-7348482c59bb.abstract: We establish uniform score bounds and Lipschitz continuity for truncated Gaussian, Cauchy, Boltzmann, and softmax policies under explicitly stated parameterizations.

2610.15789-f3fa74f6a91c.title: Inference on the Value of Policy Improvement in Adaptive Experiments
2610.15789-f3fa74f6a91c.abstract: In this paper, we develop an asymptotically normal estimator for the value of policy improvement (VPI) under adaptively collected data. This value, which is defined as the gap between the value of the best treatment policy in a class and that of a baseline policy, gauges whether or not it is worth deploying a personalized treatment policy. Building an estimator for the VPI is naturally more difficult than estimating the value of a fixed policy. This is because, in addition to contending with the correlated data and decaying propensities associated with adaptive experiments, any estimator must also handle the non-regularity, or lack of pathwise differentiability, of the underlying estimand when the optimal policy is non-unique. Our proposed estimator works by sequentially fitting a weighted empirical welfare maximizing policy on historical data and then evaluating it using inverse propensity weighting on future samples. We neither assume that the optimal policy is unique nor make a margin assumption on the underlying heterogeneous treatment effects. A key difficulty in analyzing our estimator is showing that the regret incurred through policy learning is asymptotically smaller than the standard error of the estimator. We accomplish this by showing faster regret rates for policy learning under decaying propensities, which may be of independent interest. We not only evaluate the coverage of our estimator on a mix of synthetic and semi-synthetic data, but also employ it to estimate the VPI in an adaptive experiment evaluating the efficacy of job assistance programs in Jordan due to Caria et al. Although our estimates are generally more conservative than their hierarchical Bayesian analysis, which assumes that the optimal policy is unique, we still corroborate the benefits of personalization amongst Syrian refugees.

2610.15892-9e843d21b2e3.title: Minimax Rates and Improved Spectral Convergence for Multi-Manifold Clustering
2610.15892-9e843d21b2e3.abstract: We study eigenpair estimation for the tensorized, density-weighted Laplace--Beltrami operator from $n$ independent data points sampled from a multi-manifold mixture distribution where manifolds may intersect. Let $d$ denote the largest intrinsic dimension of the manifold components and $s\geq2$ the smoothness of the sampling densities. For simple, nontrivial eigenpairs, we establish the minimax rate $n^{-s/(d+2s)}$ for approximating the eigenvalue and eigenfunction of the tensorized Laplace--Beltrami operator, and show that a continuum plug-in estimator based on kernel density estimation attains the same rate when the supporting manifolds are known. We further analyze a manifold-agnostic graph Laplacian estimator and prove that its eigenpairs converge to those of the tensorized Laplace--Beltrami operator at rate $n^{-1/(2.5d-1)}$, up to logarithmic factors, improving upon previously known spectral convergence rates for multi-manifold learning. Numerical experiments on synthetic multi-manifold data corroborate the rates guaranteed by our theorems. These results characterize the information-theoretic difficulty of multi-manifold spectral estimation and quantify the additional cost of learning without oracle component information.

2610.16030-3d0f5e428472.title: Limit Theory for Online Expectile Estimation under Short and Long Range Dependence
2610.16030-3d0f5e428472.abstract: Expectiles are tail-sensitive distributional summaries with important applications in financial risk measurement and forecasting, yet statistical theory for their online estimation from dependent data remains limited. We study a one-pass, stochastic-gradient algorithm with constant learning rate $\gamma$ for estimating the marginal expectile of a stationary causal process. The recursion admits a unique stationary causal solution and geometrically forgets its initialization. Under short-range dependence, its last iterate is asymptotically Gaussian at the $\sqrt{\gamma}$ scale, with variance governed by the population curvature and the long-run variance of the expectile score. For long-memory linear processes the scale changes to $\gamma^{\beta-1/2}\ell(1/\gamma)$, with a Gaussian limit arising from a fractional Brownian motion integral. We further derive the joint long-memory limit for multiple expectile levels and characterize its limiting covariance structure. Various numerical experiments corroborate the predicted Gaussian approximations and regime-specific fluctuation scales.

2610.16034-6adfde87fb30.title: A Nonlinear Time-Series Theory for Constant-step SGD with Momentum
2610.16034-6adfde87fb30.abstract: Constant-step stochastic gradient descent with momentum (SGDM) augments the parameter recursion with a momentum state that carries geometrically decaying memory of past stochastic gradients. We study this coupled recursion as a nonlinear time series and develop a framework for its stationary behavior and distributional limits. The joint parameter-momentum process forgets its initialization geometrically under a finite $p$th moment for $p > 1$, yielding a unique stationary causal solution. Under a second-moment condition, this contraction leads to an invariance principle and quenched Gaussian limit for averaged SGDM, while a small-learning-rate analysis gives a Gaussian limit for the last iterate. In a stochastic-curvature quadratic model, we further study how the rate of initialization forgetting relates to stationary variance and averaged fluctuations.

2610.16142-e6123d731a65.title: Distributional Regression for Arbitrary Response Variables Using ReLU Neural Networks
2610.16142-e6123d731a65.abstract: This paper develops a unified framework for distributional regression with arbitrary response variables. Rather than relying on scalar thresholds or Euclidean structure, we model conditional event probabilities indexed by measurable sets, which extends distributional regression to general response spaces while retaining a direct connection to classical event-based formulations. Within this framework, we study two complementary estimators: a preliminary estimator based on separate regression of event indicators, and a constrained estimator that enforces inclusion-consistent predictions through a directed acyclic graph (DAG) over a finite set family. We establish general error bounds for both estimators and further specialize the results to dense ReLU networks, yielding explicit convergence rates overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Simulation studies and real-data experiments further demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed framework.

2610.16149-f25cd42cd49d.title: Equilibrium Learning in Unbounded Stochastic Games with Gaussian Transitions
2610.16149-f25cd42cd49d.abstract: Learning equilibria from data is difficult when several decision makers interact indefinitely and the system state has no prescribed bounds. We examine discounted general-sum stochastic games with compact action sets and an unknown nonlinear drift observed through Gaussian transition noise. The proposed procedure uses a single uninterrupted trajectory to update Gaussian-process models of the drift and to solve successively refined finite games. We prove a perturbation result showing that stability of equilibrium selection, together with uniform KL accuracy of Gaussian transition models, is sufficient for regional uniform convergence of the induced values and approximate Nash behavior in the original game. The region specifies where the guarantees are evaluated; strategies and dynamics continue to act on the entire Euclidean state space. For GP estimators, simultaneous confidence bounds yield a rate controlled by posterior uncertainty, kernel information gain, and joint-state dimension. Numerical studies illustrate how kernel choice and dimension appear in the predicted convergence behavior.

2610.16187-5394da2a3fc1.title: Exploration strategies for Gaussian process bandit optimization with inference regret guarantees
2610.16187-5394da2a3fc1.abstract: Existing cumulative regret guarantees for Bayesian optimization (BO) do not necessarily characterize the quality of the algorithm's final output. This gap is critical under noisy evaluations, where the goal is to return a single high-quality recommendation. To address it, we introduce efficient exploration strategies that can be incorporated into any BO procedure by occasionally replacing the acquisition query with an exploration query. To validate this approach, we bound the Gaussian process posterior standard deviation over the search space via the fill distance of the queries, which measures the largest region left unexplored. We then use this result to derive upper bounds on the inference regret, i.e., the gap between the global optimum and the function value at the algorithm's returned point. Empirically, these exploration strategies improve the final recommendations of existing BO algorithms on synthetic benchmarks, hyperparameter optimization, and a control task.

2610.16285-600dfe516f48.title: Moment-Based Anomaly Detection in High-Dimensional Mixed Data
2610.16285-600dfe516f48.abstract: We propose an anomaly detection method for high-dimensional mixed-type data that maps heterogeneous features to a common scale via standardized moment-based transformations, yielding interpretable feature-level anomaly scores. These scores are combined through a dependence-aware aggregation step to construct the Mixed-data Influence (MDI) score, accounting for correlations across features and providing a unified measure of how strongly an observation departs from the reference data distribution. By incorporating higher-order moments, the MDI can detect anomalies that arise not only from location shifts, but also from changes in variability, skewness, and other distributional characteristics. The aggregation mechanism allows our method to capture both sparse anomalies concentrated in a small number of features and weak, coordinated deviations distributed across many features. We empirically investigate the distribution and thresholding behavior of the MDI score across different sample sizes, dimensions, dependence structures, and data types. Simulation experiments and two real-data applications, to multi-omics and ESG data, evaluate finite-sample calibration, detection performance, and feature-level interpretability.

2610.16447-02a1c921a1ce.title: Explaining Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Causal Forests and the Hoeffding Functional Decomposition
2610.16447-02a1c921a1ce.abstract: The estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects is a central objective of causal inference. However, state-of-the-art algorithms to solve this task are based on machine learning principles, and thus behave as black boxes. Consequently, the identification of covariates driving heterogeneity remains a challenging and open problem. To address this limitation, we introduce CausalTreeHFD, an interpretable extension of causal forests, based on the Hoeffding functional decomposition adapted to tree ensembles. Our approach decomposes predictions of conditional average treatment effects (CATE) into contributions from individual covariates and pairwise interactions, providing a direct characterization of the factors driving treatment effect heterogeneity. We establish the consistency of CausalTreeHFD, which converges towards the Hoeffding decomposition of the underlying CATE function, under standard assumptions for the analysis of causal forests. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show that CausalTreeHFD accurately identifies relevant covariates and interactions, and precisely recovers their contributions to heterogeneous treatment effects.

2610.16464-580cae3045db.title: Online Individualized Treatment Selection under Partial Feedback: False Discovery Control and Minimax Optimality
2610.16464-580cae3045db.abstract: We study online individualized treatment selection when only the outcome under the assigned treatment is observed. Our objective is to preferentially treat individuals whose potential outcomes under treatment exceed a covariate-specific control reference, while limiting false discoveries among treated individuals. We propose Partial-Feedback Adaptive Individualized Treatment Selection (PAITS), which initializes learning from historical data and combines sequential estimation of local null risks, randomized exploration, and feedback-driven updates of the treatment selection threshold. Under regularity conditions, we establish asymptotic false discovery rate control and sublinear gap-weighted assignment regret relative to a population oracle. We further establish a minimax lower bound on assignment regret under prescribed uniform nuisance-estimation requirements and give conditions under which PAITS attains the corresponding constrained minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. These results quantify the tradeoff between accurate treatment assignment and nuisance learning under partial feedback. Simulation studies and a real-data analysis using the Jester recommendation dataset illustrate the finite-sample performance of PAITS.

2610.16574-ecaf6b9ca711.title: $\texttt{NFDiag}$: High-dimensional MCMC Convergence Diagnosis with Normalizing Flows
2610.16574-ecaf6b9ca711.abstract: Accurately assessing the convergence of Monte Carlo Markov Chains is crucial for ensuring their validity in Bayesian inference problems. However, convergence assessment in high dimensions is known to be difficult, due to most convergence diagnostics becoming insensitive beyond a few dozen parameters. Conventional convergence statistics analyze marginal distributions which in high dimensions neglects increasing levels of information from the joint and conditional probability distributions. Thus we propose $\texttt{NFDiag}$, which taps into the information of the full multivariate joint posterior with a normalizing flow (NF). Our convergence diagnostic thereby also analyzes information from conditional distributions. In other words, by working in the full multivariate space, it is sensitive with respect to the geometry of the chain in high dimensions. Our diagnostic utilizes that NFs assume independent and identically distributed (iid) training samples, which is a testable assumption that will be violated by a non-converged or strongly correlated chain. Our diagnostic trains NFs on separate parts of a chain, and then assesses whether these correspond to the same multivariate target distribution. We test our diagnostic in up to 250 dimensions, and demonstrate it is universal and unbiased, and detects problematic chain quality also when Gelman-Rubin $\hat{R}$ and the multivarite effective sample size do not.

2610.16578-c062c0dae7a5.title: Variational Filtering for Bayesian Last Layers with an Independent Binary Probit Surrogate
2610.16578-c062c0dae7a5.abstract: Modern deep classifiers trained by gradient descent need many passes over the data to become accurate, and even then are not always well calibrated; post-hoc temperature scaling corrects calibration after training but cannot influence training-time accuracy or convergence. We propose a variational filtering algorithm for the last layer of deep classifiers, whose parameters are treated as the latent state of a linear-Gaussian state-space model. Each mini-batch is assimilated by an exact prediction step followed by a closed-form variational update, made conjugate by an independent binary probit (IBProbit) surrogate for the categorical likelihood. The filter's process noise stabilises the updates under feature drift and keeps the predictive distribution from collapsing to a point estimate, allowing the same procedure to be used for linear probing on a frozen backbone and for full-network fine-tuning. We evaluate on DINOv3 backbones against two baselines tuned under an identical protocol: AdamW with cross-entropy and post-hoc temperature scaling, and Variational Bayesian Last Layers (VBLL). As a linear probe on frozen features, IBProbit attains the best accuracy and negative log-likelihood on all five downstream tasks at the largest backbone, and on two of the five at the smallest. In out-of-distribution detection with CIFAR probes on the largest backbone, IBProbit reduces the false-positive rate at 95\% true-positive rate by a factor of 1.4 to 3.2 relative to the better of the two baselines, on all three dataset pairs. When the whole network is fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k, IBProbit reaches the final performance of the cross-entropy baseline in half the wall-clock time.

2610.16669-3429a4e12e7e.title: Amortized Variational Inference of Latent Intensities from Replicated Point Patterns
2610.16669-3429a4e12e7e.abstract: Bayesian inference for latent point process intensities often relies on per-dataset sampling or optimization, making repeated inference computationally expensive. We propose a neural-network-based amortized variational framework that learns a reusable inference rule mapping a variable number of replicated point patterns to a distribution over their shared latent intensity. Trained from event times using the point process likelihood, the model learns an amortized inference rule without ground-truth intensity supervision. At test time, it performs inference of the latent distribution in a forward pass. On synthetic data, additional realizations improve intensity recovery and yield narrower credible intervals with broadly stable coverage. Our method is tested on bicycle-sharing data and achieves the highest mean held-out log likelihood among the evaluated methods while requiring substantially less inference time than the Log-Gaussian Cox Process baseline.

2610.16736-e1085cebec8b.title: Amortised adaptive importance sampling
2610.16736-e1085cebec8b.abstract: Monte Carlo sampling algorithms aim to produce samples from a target distribution with a given unnormalised probability density function. The high cost of running Monte Carlo algorithms, with many simulation steps or particles needed to obtain a good empirical approximation to the target, can be reduced by introducing learnable components into the sampler -- a form of amortisation. Once these components are trained, amortised samplers can produce high-quality samples with less computation at sampling time than training-free algorithms would require. We propose an amortised sampler built upon the framework of adaptive importance sampling -- a hierarchical importance sampling procedure where the proposal is iteratively adapted. Our amortised adaptive importance sampling algorithm fits a lightweight neural network that adapts the proposal using information obtained over the course of sampling. By training our sampler over many different targets taken from the same family of distributions, we obtain a sampler that can adapt to a specific target at sampling time without a priori access to the target's parameters. We show that our procedure can efficiently sample from targets within the family the sampler was trained on, giving improvements over target-specific amortised samplers and training-free adaptive importance sampling algorithms. We also explore the potential for generalisation, where the trained sampler is used to sample from targets outwith its training family.

2610.16801-366ac8a0066d.title: When Repeated Measurements Hurt Tabular Foundation Models
2610.16801-366ac8a0066d.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on IID benchmarks, but how do they respond to repeated measurements at the same inputs? Across six TFMs, synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments show that additional measurements can improve predictions at measured inputs while degrading them elsewhere. Harm is most frequent at low noise, and irrelevant features amplify it in several models; real repeated-measurement datasets show similar patterns. Statistically, the IID rule targeted by PFN pretraining treats each repeated input as fresh evidence about the input distribution. When the prior links this distribution to the response function, the resulting protocol mismatch can outweigh the benefit of additional measurements, even under exact inference. Computationally, interventions identify row-count dependence in TabPFN-v3's attention scaling as a contributor to harm. Resetting the count largely reverses distortion in a noiseless linear diagnostic and attenuates amplification by irrelevant features. Finally, we evaluate ways to retain the benefits of repeated measurements while limiting their harm. Averaging measurements usually outperforms supplying them separately at larger repetition counts, whereas count reset can suppress both harm and useful gains. Code, saved results and reproduction instructions are available at https://github.com/drizmiz/PFN-Repeated-Measurement-Supp

2610.16815-ebd18fcc0d1a.title: On the Calibration of Crowdsourcing Aggregators
2610.16815-ebd18fcc0d1a.abstract: Calibration has been extensively studied for classifiers, but remains largely unexplored for crowdsourcing aggregation methods, which are increasingly used for making probabilistic decisions. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first theoretical and empirical study of calibration in label aggregation. To our great surprise, we find that widely used aggregation methods can be severely miscalibrated, and in opposite directions: Majority Vote is underconfident while model-based aggregators are overconfident. We prove that the Bayesian aggregator is perfectly calibrated under its data-generating model. We also show that exact calibration of weighted majority votes requires highly restrictive conditions, which helps explain why Majority Vote is generally miscalibrated in realistic crowds. Empirically, we study calibration across $39$ human crowdsourcing datasets and LLM-based crowds. In both cases, we observe systematic miscalibration for aggregation models such as Majority Vote, Dawid--Skene, GLAD, and CrowdFM. Finally, we propose a post-hoc calibration procedure that \emph{aggregates the aggregators}: for any aggregation function $\phi$, we introduce a transformation that first combines its predictive distribution with those of complementary aggregators, before applying temperature scaling. This simple and interpretable transformation makes temperature scaling more effective than when applied directly to $\phi$. It improves calibration, especially in the high-redundancy regime where there are many annotations per item, while generally preserving or even improving accuracy.

2610.16820-d3724b639478.title: Sample-Size Extrapolation in Simulation-Based Inference via Statistical Scaling
2610.16820-d3724b639478.abstract: In simulation-based inference (SBI), neural posterior estimators trained on a bounded range of sample sizes can become inaccurate on larger datasets because their parameterizations do not specify how posterior location, uncertainty and shape must change as observations accumulate. We propose center-estimated NPE (CE-NPE), which combines a statistical center with an explicit contraction rate and learns a local center correction and residual densities in posterior-scale coordinates. The center is a statistical estimate, such as a closed-form statistic or a simulator-based moment match, which does not require an evaluable likelihood. Our analysis explains how contraction amplifies center error and decomposes Gaussian posterior error into shape, mean and covariance contributions. On six regular benchmarks, CE-NPE gives the best reference-posterior agreement of all tested amortized estimators at every out-of-range size, up to five times the largest training size, without retraining; it also fits better within the training range on most of them. Matched controls and nonregular examples characterize the scope of these gains and identify the conditions on which they depend: an appropriate contraction rate, an accurate center, and a stable residual representation.

2610.16845-64cc93987f80.title: Feature Normalization under Finite Training Budgets
2610.16845-64cc93987f80.abstract: Standardizing a rare feature can help stochastic gradient descent learn its effect within a finite budget, but it also changes the noise cost of learning. We characterize the lowest rare-subgroup risks attainable by standardized and unscaled training when each chooses a nonnegative constant learning rate and a deterministic stopping time under the same observation cap. For two independent binary features, we derive both optimized risks as prevalence vanishes while the expected number of rare observations remains finite. Uniform control over rates and stopping times reduces each limiting oracle to a scalar minimization. With positive noise, the preferred scaling changes exactly once as we move signal to the rare feature while the limiting risk at initialization stays fixed and positive. The formulas also explain how noise and budget affect the comparison. Separate finite-prevalence bounds favor standardization on a rare-dominant signal family and unscaled training on a common-dominant family. The results concern final iterates with population preprocessing and fresh observations. Exact-moment searches assess the approximation at finite prevalence. In a controlled study, both orderings persist under observation reuse, estimated preprocessing, and intercept fitting when tuning choices are fixed before evaluation. Selecting a predictor after observing training can reverse an ordering, even when selection uses exact population risk.

2610.16923-5827ea13fdb9.title: Minimax Optimality of Shampoo for Nonstationary Stochastic Optimization
2610.16923-5827ea13fdb9.abstract: We develop a comprehensive theoretical analysis of Matrix Shampoo for tracking time-varying optima in nonstationary stochastic optimization. We derive finite-horizon high-probability bounds for average tracking error that disentangle initialization, optimizer drift, momentum-induced drift penalty, stochastic noise, and adaptive preconditioning, with explicit dependence on momentum parameter \(\beta_1\) and stabilization parameter \(\varepsilon\). These bounds reveal an explicit drift--noise and stability--geometry tradeoffs: noise-dominated regimes favor larger $\beta_1$, which provides stronger first-moment averaging and greater suppression of gradient noise, whereas drift-dominated regimes favor smaller $\beta_1$, allowing faster adaptation to moving optimizer. Larger $\varepsilon$ reduces the preconditioner-perturbation term while weakening Shampoo's ability to exploit matrix geometry, thereby reducing adaptivity. We establish a matching minimax lower bound under squared path-variation constraint, proving the information-theoretic optimality of Shampoo over the class of causal optimization procedures. Under a constant stepsize, we establish high-probability bounds for the average projected stationarity gap along general nonstationary nonconvex objectives. We validate our theoretical findings on both synthetic and multiple real-world problems.

2610.17053-4232f557b7d5.title: Measuring Variable Importance Using Proportional Inclusive Marginal Effects
2610.17053-4232f557b7d5.abstract: Shapley-based measures are widely used for measuring variable importance in statistics and machine learning. However, these measures have a serious issue--a nonactive variable can get a positive importance measure when it is correlated with an active variable. Herin et al. recently proposed a measure called proportional marginal effects (PME) that mitigates this spurious effect. However, PME is developed for deterministic models and has high computational cost. In this article, we propose a new measure called proportional inclusive marginal effects (PRIME) that overcomes these two limitations of PME. The key idea in PRIME is to use a novel model-free variable selection technique to identify the active variables and include only them in the computation of the importance measure. Analysis of test functions and real datasets show that PRIME can accurately and reliably quantify variable importance from noisy input-output data.

2610.17061-122814f2323d.title: In-context classification: Calibration and noise in linear attention with softmax readout
2610.17061-122814f2323d.abstract: We study in-context binary classification in a simple attention model trained to minimise a logistic loss. Each prompt has a latent logistic teacher, and the learner must infer its direction from Bernoulli-labeled context examples. We derive an asymptotic prediction for the test logit in a high-dimensional regime with context length proportional to token dimension, and total training prompts proportional to dimension squared. Our formula cleanly separates calibration, test-time context noise, and non-isotropic parameter-estimation noise as interpretable effects on in-context performance. Our analysis also identifies the ridgeless separability regime and addresses the effects of context length, pretraining-set size, regularisation, and sampling temperature on in-context classification performance. The theory's predictions closely agree with finite-dimensional simulations and fully trained linear-attention models, while experiments with standard softmax attention show qualitatively related behaviour beyond the regime assumed by our analysis.

2610.17146-9a6ce2f83677.title: SCOPE Before You Sample: Conformal Scores Guide Posterior Exploration for Fast and Calibrated Bayesian Predictive Inference
2610.17146-9a6ce2f83677.abstract: Bayesian predictive regions account for parameter uncertainty but can be poorly calibrated under model misspecification, even with expensive full MCMC. Cheaper approximations such as variational inference reduce the cost but often yield less accurate predictive distributions. We propose SCOPE (Score-guided Conformal Posterior Exploration), which retains the predictive quality of full MCMC while achieving calibrated coverage at a fraction of its cost. The key observation is that a prediction region can depend on the posterior mainly through a few parameter directions that move the region's boundary, and these are generally not the directions of largest posterior variance. SCOPE gives nonconformity scores a new role in guiding posterior computation: score gradients on a held-out guide set, weighted toward the target boundary, identify the relevant directions. MCMC explores this subspace, while an inexpensive projected variational approximation carries the remaining uncertainty. The same guide set calibrates the region's final density level. We establish asymptotic coverage for SCOPE and provide a split variant with finite-sample validity. Controlled simulations show that score-guided exploration yields more accurate calibrated regions than non-targeted direction choices at low active rank. Across simulated and real benchmarks, SCOPE has a median test-NLL gap of only 0.002 nats relative to full Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), and on the real benchmarks it runs 12-15 times faster.

2610.17159-2f9a9ad8b58e.title: A Generalized McDiarmid Inequality: Sample Reuse and Non-Uniform Unbounded Differences
2610.17159-2f9a9ad8b58e.abstract: We develop a novel generalization of McDiarmid's concentration inequality and use it to obtain a uniform law of large numbers result and error bounds on stochastic optimization problems which simultaneously incorporate two key features: 1) They capture the benefit of training sample reuse in algorithms that also employ easily-sampled auxiliary random variables. 2) They allow for one-component mean-difference bounding functions which are both unbounded in the component of interest and have non-uniform dependence on another component. We demonstrate the utility of our method by deriving concentration inequalities for score-based generative modeling. This application naturally leverages both key features of our new tools: 1) It utilizes auxiliary Gaussian random variables in conjunction with the training samples; accounting for training sample reuse results in tighter error bounds by effectively integrating out the dependence on the auxiliary random variables. 2) The ability to handle non-uniform mean-difference bounding functions allows us to treat unbounded score models and data distributions with unbounded support.

2610.17316-a1c6771e5e1f.title: Deeply unrolled alternating projections for phase retrieval
2610.17316-a1c6771e5e1f.abstract: Deep unrolling methods for inverse problems augment traditional reconstruction algorithms with learned priors to improve their performance. These methods have been developed under the implicit assumption that the geometry of the measurement operator does not change between training and deployment; when this is no longer the case, the quality of obtained reconstructions can degrade significantly. In this paper, we argue that this is not an inherent limitation of the deep unrolling paradigm and can be mitigated by a careful choice of the underlying iterative algorithm. We propose a deep unrolling framework for the phase retrieval problem that augments the alternating projections method with a learned denoising step. Our method obtains high-quality reconstructions without the need for retraining in settings where conventional model-based alternatives struggle, such as when the dynamic range of the measurement operator changes significantly at test time.

2610.17333-0384693da0da.title: Accounting for model error in ensemble variational data assimilation through learned generative dynamics
2610.17333-0384693da0da.abstract:
Many approaches have recently been proposed to combine data assimilation with machine learning for improved forecasts with geophysical models. Here, we focus on combining advanced sequential data assimilation schemes with a generative forecasting model which accounts for complex model errors. This generative model provides a stochastic approximation of the conditional distribution of the successor state given the current state. The proposed variational formulation is a novel one-step weak-constraint 4D-Var scheme in which a learned conditional stochastic forecast replaces the prescribed additive Gaussian model error representation. We derive and implement this formulation as an ensemble variational algorithm, the generative iterative ensemble Kalman filter (IEnKF-G), which generalises the iterative ensemble Kalman filter with additive Gaussian model error (IEnKF-Q). We extend the method to a smoother with an assimilation window spanning multiple time steps and propose a simplified variant.
  The IEnKF-G is evaluated on a stochastic variant of the Lorenz 1963 model to assess its robustness. It is then tested on a multi-scale variant of the one-dimensional Lorenz 1996 model, in which the resolved variables are affected by model error originating from the hidden small-scale variables. The algorithm is then compared to an ensemble Kalman filter that adaptively mitigates model and sampling errors, and to the IEnKF-Q. The IEnKF-G is generally more accurate in the tested configurations, with substantial gains under partial observations and significant model error. This demonstrates the potential of generative data-driven models when paired with classical data assimilation methods, particularly when model error is substantial.

2610.17343-95249faf019b.title: Monitoring for Shifts at Unknown Times: Parameter-Free Conditional Conformal Martingales
2610.17343-95249faf019b.abstract: Conditional conformal test martingales provide sequential tests for detecting distribution shifts, using a fixed reference dataset to avoid contamination from test-time samples. Prior work used a penalized betting function via online optimization with smoothing, clipping, and other hyperparameters, which can adapt slowly when a shift occurs after a long stationary period. In this work, we introduce an approach that requires no hyperparameters and provably adapts quickly to shifts occurring at unknown times. Our key idea is to frame the penalized betting problem as portfolio selection in a three-asset market. Then, we use a restarting universal portfolio, with a heavy-tailed wealth allocation over time. We establish anytime false-alarm control and derive optimal finite-sample bounds on detection delay under detectable alternatives. We also develop an FFT-based implementation that computes the portfolio sequence over $T$ rounds in $\mathcal{O}(T^2\ln T)$ time, instead of $\mathcal{O}(T^3)$ of the naive implementation. Synthetic and real-world experiments suggest that the proposed approach adapts rapidly after long periods of null samples, with detection delays depending substantially less on shift time than prior baselines.

2610.17579-6cf21f2c059c.title: Risk-Averse Inference-Time Diffusion Model Alignment with Finite-Sample Guarantees
2610.17579-6cf21f2c059c.abstract: Inference-time alignment steers diffusion models toward downstream objectives without costly fine-tuning, but existing methods typically optimize expected cost (or reward) without explicitly controlling tail risk. In this work, we propose a risk-averse framework for inference-time alignment of diffusion models that balances expected cost and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) under trajectory-level Kullback-Leibler regularization. We characterize the optimal path distribution and reverse transitions as functions of the CVaR threshold, reducing the alignment problem to a one-dimensional optimization problem over the threshold. We show that this one-dimensional optimization problem can be nonconvex in general, establish sufficient conditions for convexity, and introduce quadratic regularization to enable efficient derivative-free ternary search. Under suitable assumptions, we provide finite-sample guarantees for threshold optimization and value estimation, and combine them into a terminal total-variation bound relative to the regularized target under exact resampling. Experiments on synthetic data and image generation using Stable Diffusion demonstrate improved tail performance over risk-neutral baselines while maintaining competitive average cost.

2610.17655-7c4ca38c8175.title: textGrain watermarking is harder to detect: can sum-tests still do it optimally?
2610.17655-7c4ca38c8175.abstract: Watermarking embeds an imperceptible signal in text from large language models that is statistically detectable with a secret key. The recent textGrain watermark (Li et. al. (2026b)) calibrates this signal against the model's sampling entropy through an explicit entropy budget, combining the stochasticity of Red-Green and the unbiasedness of Gumbel-max watermarks, and its accompanying report proposes a detector that sums pivotal statistics. We study when, and how efficiently, textGrain can be detected after human edits, modeled as a sparse mixture in which a fraction $\varepsilon_n\asymp n^{-p}$ of positions retain the watermark and token uncertainty decays as $n^{-q}$. First, entropy calibration comes at a cost: the minimax detection boundary of textGrain is $p+q=1/2$, so its detectable region is strictly smaller than that of Gumbel-max and maximal-coupling watermarks, whose boundary is $2p+q=1$. This cost stems from textGrain's construction rather than from entropy calibration itself: an unbiased scheme with the same entropy loss remains detectable where textGrain is not. Second, perhaps surprisingly, this loss makes the sum detector optimal at the boundary when the number of transport columns is fixed, unlike for Gumbel-max. When the number of columns grows and the entropy budget does not vanish, the detectable region expands while that of the sum detector does not. Third, for a fixed edit fraction, we characterize the optimal exponential rate of type II error decay and show that the sum detector falls strictly short of it at every fixed alternative. Finally, we propose a weighted multiscale binomial scan, valid in finite samples and needing no knowledge of the next-token distributions, entropy budget, or edit fraction; it attains every detection boundary above and the optimal exponent.

2610.17956-37f00cf1019e.title: Learning Distributions from Samples and Qualities
2610.17956-37f00cf1019e.abstract: We study parameter estimation when each sample from a continuous parametric distribution is accompanied by a binary quality label governed by the same unknown parameter. By imposing hard feasibility constraints, deterministic labels can accelerate estimation from the classical $n^{-1/2}$ rate of smooth quality-aware M-estimators to $n^{-1}$. Combining PAC guarantees with local error-to-parameter conversions, we establish this rate for both identifiable and finitely ambiguous quality classifiers, with likelihood information resolving the latter ambiguity. When the quality model is known only up to an additive constant, we construct threshold-free pairwise preferences from oppositely labeled samples and retain the accelerated rate despite the unknown threshold. We further show that pointwise qualities and pairwise preferences are incomparable: either can be strictly more informative than the other. Our assumptions hold for Gaussian, Laplace, and exponential families under thresholded log-likelihood rewards. Finally, a minimax lower bound establishes the optimal $n^{-1}$ dependence on sample size, up to logarithmic and dimension-dependent factors, while experiments confirm the benefits of constraint-based estimation.

2610.18037-4c2df37754f6.title: Weighting-Based Strategies for Classification: Analysis and Local Peak Dynamics with CART Trees
2610.18037-4c2df37754f6.abstract: Tabular learning tasks often suffer from class imbalance, which is often addressed via weighting-based strategies. In this work, we compare the naive approach (unweighted) with the weighting-based rebalancing strategies. Somewhat surprisingly, we demonstrate that, asymptotically, as the predictor complexity increases with sample size, weighting strategies yield predictive performance identical to unweighted approaches across all evaluation metrics, up to a shift in the final threshold. To go beyond, we theoretically study the estimation of a linear regression function through weighted and unweighted CART trees with limited depths. In this setting, we prove that the points in the PR space for both strategies are distributed along the same curve, thus illustrating the similar nonasymptotic performance of the two strategies. Then, we numerically identify more complex synthetic settings where performance gaps, evaluated via fixed classifier complexity, favor weighting strategies. Thus, to guide practitioners, we introduce an indicator that aims at signaling whether a data set may benefit from weighting.

2610.18055-bc71dae7429f.title: Reliable Scale-Free Bandits via Empirical Likelihood
2610.18055-bc71dae7429f.abstract: We study stochastic bandits without knowledge of reward scales or tail parameters. Almost-sure regret guarantees describe eventual learning but do not quantify expected performance or the risk of large regret in a finite run. We introduce $\texttt{EL-F}$, an anytime empirical-likelihood (EL) extension of the $g$-Forcing policy of Cowan and Katehakis (2020), and characterize its performance at three levels. First, for integrable rewards and non-decreasing, diverging exploration schedules $g$ with vanishing increments, $\texttt{EL-F}$ preserves the $g$-Forcing asymptotics for pseudo-regret $R(T)$: $R(T)/g(T)\to\sum_{i:\Delta_i>0}\Delta_i$ almost surely as $T\to\infty$, where $\Delta_i$ is the suboptimality gap of arm $i$. Second, on every sub-exponential instance, for non-decreasing $g(t)=\omega(\log t)$ satisfying a mild feasibility condition, expected pseudo-regret is at most $g(T)\sum_{i:\Delta_i>0}\Delta_i+C_{\underline{P}}$, where $C_{\underline{P}}$ is an instance-dependent constant independent of $T$. Moreover, we also establish finite-time tail bounds with super-polynomial decay in regret beyond the forced-exploration budget. For slowly varying $g$, we determine the exact exponent of linear regret deviations on two-armed Gaussian instances with common variance and establish a matching lower bound among policies satisfying the same expected-regret budget on every such Gaussian instance. These quantitative guarantees also cover the greedy variant obtained at zero EL radius. A fixed positive radius introduces local optimism while preserving the leading asymptotic regret. We establish coupled pathwise dominance over the greedy variant in two-armed bandits with a deterministic suboptimal arm. Experiments demonstrate reductions in prolonged suboptimal allocation compared with $g$-Forcing on challenging instances.

2610.18166-603b9f462004.title: Lifting Finite-Sample Gaussian Approximation of Wide Neural Networks to Functional Convergence
2610.18166-603b9f462004.abstract: Randomly initialised neural networks of width $m$ converge to Gaussian processes as $m \to \infty$, with two types of quantitative bounds characterising this convergence. Finite-sample bounds compare the network with its Gaussian limit at a fixed finite sample set, on an arbitrary domain, in the quadratic Wasserstein distance $\mathcal W_2$, achieving a convergence rate of $m^{-1/2}$ with explicit constants. However, these constants grow with the number of samples, so the bound becomes uninformative as the sample set is refined. Functional bounds remove that dependence by comparing the two as random functions, at the price of spherical input, metrics weaker than $\mathcal W_2$, or slower rates. In this paper, we therefore lift a finite-sample bound to a functional one. The lifting refines the sample set until it is dense in the domain, so the bound must first be made independent of the number of samples. We achieve this by measuring the error per sample, which makes the constant uniform. For a polynomial activation and any compact input set, this gives a rate of $m^{-1/2}$ in the supremum norm, with an explicit constant.

2610.18196-77f83d4871eb.title: Hierarchical Time Series Forecasting with Operator-Valued Kernels
2610.18196-77f83d4871eb.abstract: Hierarchical time series forecasting requires generating accurate predictions that are coherent across multiple levels of aggregation. Existing methods either rely on two-stage pipelines with post-hoc reconciliation or on end-to-end models that often lack statistical guarantees. We introduce a unified framework that formulates hierarchical forecasting as a multivariate regression problem in a vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert space. By designing structured operator-valued kernels, our approach enforces coherence directly within the hypothesis space, ensuring that all predictions satisfy hierarchical constraints by construction. We further propose tailored kernel constructions for hierarchical data and derive excess risk bounds that characterize generalization performance. Empirical results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the relevance of the proposed method.

2610.18333-fc3df3954892.title: On the Optimality of Random Features under General Conditions: Misspecified Cases and Robust Learning
2610.18333-fc3df3954892.abstract: Random features provide a standard approach to scaling kernel methods to large datasets by approximating the kernel with a finite-dimensional feature map. Existing works of random feature methods primarily focus on well-specified models and light-tailed noise conditions, leaving a gap in understanding their performance under more general conditions, such as misspecified models and heavy-tailed noise. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive and improved analysis of kernel ridge regression with random features (KRR-RF) under general conditions. In the light-tailed noise setting, we improve upon the worst-case uniform bounds of the feature map used in the previous works and lead to the minimax optimal learning rates with $2r+\gamma>\alpha_0$, where $(r,\gamma,\alpha_0)$ denote the regularity of the target function, the effective dimension of the kernel, and the embedding index of the RKHS, respectively. In the heavy-tailed noise setting, we leverage a recently developed Hilbert-valued Fuk-Nagaev inequality and extend the same optimal results under finite weak moment conditions. The additional cost to achieve robustness is a mildly stronger explicit sample-size requirement than in the light-tailed case. For both settings, our results recover the conditions random features budgets (up to log factors) required in the previous works. In the most benign case when $\alpha_0=\gamma$, KRR-RF are minimax optimal for all $r \in (0,1]$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to establish optimal learning rates for KRR-RF under weak moment conditions in the misspecified setting. Numerical experiments and a real data analysis validate the derived learning rates and demonstrate their practical relevance in the presence of mis-specification and heavy-tailed noise.

2610.18434-c41586652568.title: Convergence-Rate-Guided Algorithm Design of Expected Improvement for Continuous Simulation Optimization
2610.18434-c41586652568.abstract: Expected improvement (EI) based on stochastic kriging (SK) surrogate is widely used in continuous simulation optimization, but unknown heteroscedastic noise on simulation output makes three basic design choices consequential: the incumbent used to define improvement, the replication level at each sampled point, and the terminal recommendation. Existing methods typically either assume the noise levels are known or choose these components separately through heuristic rules or empirical calibration. We instead derive a high-probability upper bound on the simple regret and systematically choose the three components within general rule classes to tighten this bound. We first establish a finite-sample confidence bound for the SK predictor with unknown and estimated noise levels as a foundation for the three design choices. We then analyze general posterior-quantile families for both the incumbent and the terminal recommendation. For the incumbent, minimizing the regret bound selects a lower quantile coefficient that matches the coefficient in the SK predictor confidence bound. For the terminal recommendation, minimizing the same bound instead selects the sampled point with the best upper posterior quantile under the same coefficient. These opposite quantile choices reflect the different roles of search and implementation in simulation optimization. Intermediate simulations are exploratory with an optimistic incumbent, while the terminal recommendation is implemented in the real system and is therefore relatively conservative about the remaining posterior uncertainty. Under mild conditions satisfied by common kernels, minimizing a tractable kernel-specific bound yields $\Theta(\log T)$ replications. To our knowledge, this is the first simple-regret guarantee for a continuous-domain EI-type simulation optimization method that learns unknown heteroscedastic variances through replications.

2610.18504-d28270fc9e43.title: How Low Can You Go: Fine-Tuning LLMs with Bayesian Optimization (LlMBO)
2610.18504-d28270fc9e43.abstract: Recently, Morris et al. introduced TinyLoRA, a strategy for LLM fine-tuning which introduces arbitrarily few parameters, and demonstrated accuracy improvements using less than $10$ parameters rather than the ${\gtrsim 10,000}$ typically demanded by LoRA-based methods. However, that study continued to use gradient-based local search methods of the kind deployed for training multi-billion parameter LLMs in the first place. This article is predicated on the observation that, in the low dimensional setting, global optimization methods become tractable, unlocking Large language Model Bayesian Optimization (LlMBO). LlMBO is sample-efficient, gradient-free, memory-light, parallelizes across devices without synchronization, and, unlike policy-gradient methods, can optimize greedy-decoding accuracy directly. We describe numerical experiments comparing LlMBO against GRPO on fine-tuning tasks for a variety of models on a math benchmark suite which show that LlMBO can be a suitable alternative in this regime, matching or exceeding GRPO's fine tuning gains, while using a fraction of the compute and memory.

2610.18551-e8c42f80b9d6.title: Understanding Circulant Permutation to Extend the CMinHash Estimator
2610.18551-e8c42f80b9d6.abstract: CMinHash promises a new direction for designing MinHash algorithms with reduced variance and storage space via circulant permutations. However, the original variance analysis is difficult to extend to other MinHash estimators. We present a new approach that gives explicit and easily comparable approximate variance expressions, and use it to analyze the Minner estimator. Numerical experiments show that our variance expression matches the empirical mean square error (MSE) of estimates. Our work thereby demonstrates how to apply circulant permutation to other MinHash estimators and compute their approximate variance.

2610.18825-0dc80ffe6baa.title: Joint Neural Posterior Estimation and Model Selection for Chemical Reaction Networks
2610.18825-0dc80ffe6baa.abstract: Simulation-based Bayesian inference for Chemical Reaction Networks (CRNs) must simultaneously solve two computationally demanding problems: discriminating between overlapping reaction pathways and estimating reaction rate constants. Classical approaches, such as Sequential Monte Carlo ABC, rely on handcrafted summary statistics and scale poorly across large parameter spaces. To overcome this, we introduce a neural inference architecture. Our pipeline utilizes shared 1D-CNNs and a permutation-invariant Set Attention mechanism to learn low-dimensional summary statistics from variable-length, multi-experiment time-series data. These statistics simultaneously condition a model selection network to compute posterior model probabilities and model-specific conditional Invertible Neural Networks (cINNs) that estimate parameter posterior distributions. We demonstrate the practical utility of our approach on a real protodeboronation example, illustrating how it handles structural ambiguity and extracts kinetic parameters from competing catalyst deactivation pathways.

2610.13982-332f5fc13eb5.title: PRIME: Frequency-Aware Unified Pruning and Merging for MoE Compression
2610.13982-332f5fc13eb5.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have emerged as an effective paradigm for scaling large language models, yet their massive parameter footprint poses severe memory challenges for deployment. Existing compression methods typically treat expert pruning and merging as disjoint operations and rely on greedy heuristics, often leading to irreversible information loss or representational pollution. In this paper, we propose PRIME, a unified optimization framework for MoE compression via adaptive PRunIng and MErging. PRIME casts the discrete prune-merge assignment step as a global Integer Linear Programming over a frequency-weighted surrogate objective, jointly selecting pruning and merging decisions while accounting for expert usage. We motivate the frequency-aware objective through an error-bound analysis under fixed representative assignments, and show that the formulation favors high-frequency experts as centroids, promoting routing stability. Extensive experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B demonstrate that PRIME achieves strong accuracy retention across knowledge, coding, math, and long-context tasks, while serving benchmarks of merged models quantify the memory and throughput benefits of expert compression in vLLM.

2610.14029-a0fc966fb6e4.title: Can We Trust This Evaluation? Instance-Level Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge
2610.14029-a0fc966fb6e4.abstract: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation commonly aggregates multiple judges' decisions into a majority vote, yet this panel decision process does not guarantee that the evaluation of an individual item is reliable. We propose Structured Cross-fitted Uncertainty Risk (SCUR), a label-free approach for estimating instance-level evaluation reliability based on the judge panel's behavior. A latent measurement model serves as the backbone for measurement system analysis, from which SCUR derives three complementary signals capturing panel uncertainty, measurement cross-entropy, and perturbation sensitivity. These three sources of evidence are combined into a risk score. We evaluate the SCUR approach on five real-world benchmarks using majority-vote error ranking, selective trust, and risk stratification. Furthermore, we show our approach to be more effective at detecting high-consensus risk items, which are the blind spots for many other LLM-as-a-judge evaluation methods.

2610.14030-05d94e47ccfe.title: Rotate the Loop: Blockwise Conformality for Looped Transformers
2610.14030-05d94e47ccfe.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one shared block across many recurrent steps, so depth becomes a quantity that can be spent at runtime rather than a stack of distinct layers. Those extra steps help only if a write made on one recurrent step is still readable on later ones, and that depends on the linear map applied to the residual between recurrent steps. We show that whether the loop learns to track state is a geometric question about the form of this map, and we propose blockwise conformal injections: the residual splits into coordinate-aligned groups and rotates inside each one, so every group has its own timescale while the geometry stays exact within it. Our experiments show a performance increase on a demanding form of state tracking - last-token accuracy when the rest of the prefix is already correct - and on language modelling, where a signal written earlier has to be retrieved at the end of the sequence.

2610.14031-b9cb1c3635da.title: PLDiv: Measuring Dataset Diversity and Semantic Collapse via Persistence Landscapes
2610.14031-b9cb1c3635da.abstract: Modern data pipelines increasingly combine human-created and human-curated data with AI-generated data for model training and evaluation. As datasets grow, they often add semantically redundant samples rather than expanding semantic coverage, which deteriorates the quality of the whole dataset. Existing diversity metrics primarily summarize lexical variation, entropy, or pairwise similarity, but provide limited characterization of the shape of the underlying data distribution. In this paper, we propose PLDiv, a diversity metric derived from persistence landscapes that quantifies the structural organization of a dataset from its geometric representation. PLDiv summarizes how data neighborhoods evolve as nearby samples progressively connect, producing an interpretable scalar measure of structural diversity without requiring task-specific supervision. Whether measuring intrinsic diversity in text generations or image embeddings, or detecting semantic collapse in instruction datasets and reasoning trajectories, PLDiv performs competitively against evaluated baselines and aligns strongly with diversity labels during semantic collapse. Consequently, it effectively supports applications in synthetic data monitoring, dataset construction, data augmentation, and generative model evaluation.

2610.14246-d5142d7eec8a.title: Learning Non-Gaussian SEMs with Conditional Risk, and Why the Direction of Recursion Matters
2610.14246-d5142d7eec8a.abstract: Variance-based methods recover a Gaussian linear structural equation model (SEM) with equal or suitably constrained error variances, either by recursively identifying the source nodes with smallest conditional variance (top-down method) or sink nodes with highest conditional variance (bottom-up method). We show that the use of conditional variance is incidental: replacing it with the conditional risk, i.e., the minimal expected loss of linear prediction under the negative log-likelihood of the noise distribution, extends both methods to non-Gaussian noise. Existing methods are the least-squares special case. This yields two main results. First, exploiting the noise distribution improves structure recovery: the matched-loss procedures recover the SEM more accurately than their least-squares counterparts and the LiNGAM methods, which are designed for non-Gaussianity. Second, the two methods, interchangeable in the Gaussian setting, separate under non-Gaussian noise: the top-down method is correct for every noise density with finite differential entropy, whereas the bottom-up method requires a regularity condition and can fail without it, for instance under mean-zero exponential or Cauchy noise. Simulations confirm both results.

2610.14260-f1c6565277ea.title: Variance Fingerprints: Component-Wise Identification of Content Factors by Augmentation Design
2610.14260-f1c6565277ea.abstract: Augmentation-based self-supervised learning can recover the content shared across views without separating its underlying factors into individual coordinates. We ask whether augmentations can be designed to make those factors identifiable. Our approach allows content factors to fluctuate across augmented views while preserving their mean for each source instance. Each instance receives a fixed, recorded set of augmentation strengths that controls how much its factors fluctuate. When factors respond differently to changes in these strengths, their patterns of variation provide information that distinguishes them. Under suitable decoder and support assumptions, we prove that these differences identify individual factors in a conditional Gaussian model, up to permutation, scaling, and translation. We then develop a learner that uses the recorded strengths to estimate these patterns jointly across instances, enabling learning from few views per instance. Synthetic experiments demonstrate near-perfect factor recovery through nonlinear mixing. Controlled dSprites experiments show improved coordinate alignment using augmentations that target known factors, even without telling the learner which augmentation corresponds to which representation coordinate. These results suggest a route to component identification in self-supervised learning: augmentation design can supply identifying information beyond shared content alone.

2610.14320-1a7b0d659cff.title: De-biased Distribution Estimation for Locally Differential Private Survival Data
2610.14320-1a7b0d659cff.abstract: Sharing time-to-event data can leak sensitive information about individual participants in clinical studies. To protect the privacy of data, differential privacy (DP) framework offers rigorous protection for data sharing. The local variant of differential privacy is particularly appealing because each record is perturbed before it leaves the data owner or contributor. However, the injected perturbation distorts the true distribution of the source data, yielding low utility and invalid statistical inference with the released data. In this work, we propose a nonparametric estimator for the true survivor function via the deconvolution kernel function with locally differential private (LDP) right-censored survival data in which both the event times and the event indicators are privatized. Our estimator simultaneously de-biases the perturbation applied to the times and the errors induced by flipping the event indicators due to LDP. Theoretically, we establish the uniform consistency and point-wise asymptotic normality of the de-biased distribution estimator, and derive its uniform convergence rate together with the optimal bandwidth attaining that rate. Simulation studies and the analysis of a semi-synthetic dataset generated from the METABRIC breast cancer cohort demonstrate the performance of the proposed estimator across privacy budgets, censoring levels, and sample sizes. By the post-processing property of DP, the proposed de-biased estimator inherits the privacy guarantee while restoring valid inference on the survivor function.

2610.14414-9a4a2d63f527.title: Prior-Informed Generalizable Low-Rank Representation Learning via Regularized Adversarial Reweighting
2610.14414-9a4a2d63f527.abstract: Modern learning problems increasingly leverage data from heterogeneous sources to improve robustness and generalizability under distribution shift, often with high-dimensional parameters admitting low-rank structure. Existing group distributionally robust optimization (group-DRO) approaches optimize against adverse source mixtures, but extending this principle to low-rank matrix estimation with a broad class of losses leads to a challenging nonconvex-concave problem for which methods and theory remain limited. We propose Prior-Informed generalizable Low-rank representation Learning via Adversarial Reweighting (PILLAR), which smooths the group-DRO objective by regularizing adversarial source weights toward a user-specified reference distribution while learning a shared low-rank representation. By tempering extreme adversarial reweighting, PILLAR improves estimation stability and reduces the potential conservativeness of group-DRO. Using Burer-Monteiro factorization, we optimize the nonconvex-concave objective by bifactored gradient descent with mirror ascent. We establish linear convergence to a statistical neighborhood of the population saddle point and derive an error bound that separates low-rank estimation from adversarial reweighting. We further show that PILLAR improves on vanilla group DRO when the latter's excess conservativeness dominates source heterogeneity and prior misspecification. Simulations and an electronic health record study of suicide-attempt risk demonstrate improved worst-source and transported predictive accuracy.

2610.14427-677079822f80.title: ByteMark: A Unified Byte-Level Watermark for Detection Across Language Models
2610.14427-677079822f80.abstract: As watermarking of LLM-generated text enters deployment, users increasingly need to check text whose source is unknown. Existing detectors read the watermark through a specific tokenizer or embedding pipeline, and even if all providers adopted the same watermarking method, differences in these representations would leave their watermarks incompatible, and the text alone does not reveal which representation produced it. We propose ByteMark, a unified watermarking scheme that defines its signal on the UTF-8 bytes of published text. Models with different tokenizers embed this signal under one public specification and key, and a single detector verifies the text from the text and key alone. When the tokenizer or embedding model of a baseline detector is replaced, its detection degrades sharply, whereas ByteMark, which uses neither, retains its detection rate; ByteMark also remains detectable when participating models continue or rewrite the text.

2610.14498-ad47a5d1d50f.title: Copula Active Subspaces II: Error Decomposition, A Posteriori Estimation, and Sharpness of the Bounds
2610.14498-ad47a5d1d50f.abstract: The Copula Active Subspaces (CAS) method of Part I estimates a non-Gaussian observation-noise density $\pi_{\boldsymbol{n}}$ from residual samples. Its KL divergence $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\boldsymbol{n}}\,\|\,\widehat\pi_{\boldsymbol{n}})$ admits an exact decomposition into marginal, projection and reduced-density terms and bounds the posterior KL divergence averaged over the true predictive distribution. We derive a priori bounds for these terms, together with estimates or bounds from residual samples. Weighted nearest-neighbour entropy estimates are used for the marginal and reduced-density terms, with asymptotic standard errors in exact rank coordinates. For the projection error, the score is fitted on one subsample, and its mean squared magnitude outside the retained subspace is estimated on the other. Corrections for score and rank-transform errors then give a theoretical upper bound with probability at least $1-\delta$. Tests on three known noise laws in dimension $d=20$ use the estimated rank transform. In $11$ of $12$ combinations of example and sample size, the sum of the two estimated terms and the trace bound exceeds the reference divergence after averaging over the estimated models. In these tests, score-estimation error is the largest contribution to looseness. The overestimate from the Gaussian log-Sobolev inequality alone is at most a factor of $1.98$.

2610.14696-78f9dc2a02b3.title: Understanding Hidden Spatial Preferences in Bayesian Optimization
2610.14696-78f9dc2a02b3.abstract: Bayesian optimization uses posterior uncertainty to decide where to explore, but this uncertainty is not spatially neutral. On bounded domains, Gaussian-process posterior variance is typically larger near faces, edges, and corners, giving variance-based acquisition functions a systematic boundary bias. This spatial preference is usually inherited from the surrogate rather than chosen as part of the exploration strategy. We separate these roles by keeping the predictive model fixed and modifying the spatial preference of the exploration term. We control the preference with spatial weight fields and amortize their construction with neural surrogates. Controlled experiments show that the Gaussian process' default boundary bias changes which parts of the domain are explored and which optima are reached. We compare three alternative exploration principles and find, across standard benchmark functions and stochastic robot-pushing tasks, that they can often lower regret, particularly early in the optimization. The spatial structure of posterior uncertainty is therefore not a neutral default: it shapes the exploration strategy and can materially affect optimization performance.

2610.14904-7c84e0888184.title: Prediction with Expert Advice under Heavy-Tailed Losses
2610.14904-7c84e0888184.abstract: We study prediction with expert advice over $T$ rounds with $K$ experts under heavy-tailed losses whose $(1+\epsilon)$-moment is bounded by $\theta>0$ for some $\epsilon\in(0,1]$. In this setting, existing algorithms designed for the case $\epsilon=1$ can be suboptimal when $\epsilon<1$, suffering an additional polynomial dependence on $K$. We characterize the minimax pseudo-regret rate as $\Theta((\theta T)^{\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}}(\log K)^{\frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}})$ and establish gap-dependent lower bounds in a self-bounded environment. To attain this minimax rate without prior knowledge of either $\epsilon$ or $\theta$, we propose Adaptive Heavy-Tailed FTRL, which uses robust data-dependent scale adaptation together with truncation. We further develop Adaptive Heavy-Tailed OMD, which likewise requires neither $\epsilon$ nor $\theta$ and achieves near-optimal regret guarantees in both adversarial and self-bounded environments. Finally, when $\epsilon$ and $\theta$ are known, an FTRL algorithm with Shannon-entropy regularization achieves optimal regret guarantees in both environments.

2610.14988-278b202f90de.title: Mixing Regularization for Average-Reward $Q$-Learning and $Q$-Planning
2610.14988-278b202f90de.abstract: The average-reward setting for reinforcement learning is challenging because its Bellman operator is known to contract in span only when the underlying Markov chain is mixing. Whereas existing work typically assumes a contraction property, e.g., through environment mixing, we consider the setting where we are given a reward-agnostic $m$-step mixing policy, and we control the contraction and exploration properties of the learned policy by regularizing toward the mixing policy. We provide finite-time analysis of $Q$-learning algorithms that can be instantiated with multiple choices of regularization, with guarantees measured with respect to the regularized fixed point. Our framework exposes novel regularizer-dependent objects that control contraction, exploration, and operator bias. In the one-step setting, our rates match the best known rates for $Q$-iteration and synchronous $Q$-learning, and for $m$-step mixing we derive new rates. We also study $Q$-planning variants, and show that planning acts as time-localized learning, where the planning horizon $H$ trades off the bias from the boundary value against the sample complexity. Finally, we present numerical studies validating the analysis: (i) knowledge of a strong mixing policy improves convergence and exploration, and its advantage increases with bottleneck severity and, (ii) our theory predicts the convergence and bias rankings of regularizers from the $\alpha$-divergence family.

2610.14989-e806be7bce50.title: Characterizing the Separability Gap in Prior-Data Fitted Networks
2610.14989-e806be7bce50.abstract: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are transformers pretrained on simulated datasets to approximate Bayesian posterior predictive distributions. Standard PFN theory assumes a separable task prior, under which the feature distribution and the mechanism generating labels from features are independent. We show that common PFN priors are non-separable, even in simple settings. Consequently, standard pretraining targets a predictive distribution based on a task posterior updated using both the labeled context and the query features. We characterize its difference from the predictive based on the context posterior alone and show that this difference vanishes under posterior concentration. Under misspecification (i.e., when the true joint distribution lies outside the prior's support), however, prior non-separability can favor better feature fit at the expense of conditional label fit. We illustrate the consequences for feature attribution, Bayesian optimization, and martingale checks of Bayesian behavior. The same dependence also enables PFNs to learn from additional unlabeled observations. We demonstrate this with SemiTabICL, a PFN explicitly pretrained to use these observations, which improves accuracy over a matched supervised baseline. Our findings highlight the need for explicit rules on unlabeled data use in PFN evaluation and establish the dependence between feature and label distributions as a consequential prior design choice.

2610.15039-dc62bab66d50.title: Sparsity Saves Compute, Not Samples: Oracle Inequalities for Dense and Sparse Mixture of Experts
2610.15039-dc62bab66d50.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine specialized experts through an input-dependent routing mechanism, and their sparse variants underpin many modern large-scale systems. Yet the statistical cost of adaptive routing remains only partially understood. We study the estimation error of least-squares MoE estimators when both the experts and the gating network are Lipschitz in their parameters. We represent each MoE as a gate--expert pair in a Gated Hilbert Space, whose norm $\|\cdot\|_\Delta$ separates the contributions of routing and expert discrepancies. Using its empirical representation, we derive an oracle inequality with a fast rate of order $\tilde{\mathcal O}\big((Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}+d_{\mathrm{pr},g})/n\big)$ for dense MoEs with $K$ experts. For sparse Top-$k$ and Top-$p$ routing, the selection map is discontinuous in the gating parameters. We handle this by partitioning the gating class according to the selection patterns it induces on the sample. The resulting bounds match the dense rate up to an additive routing cost governed by the Natarajan dimension of the selector. We show that such a routing-complexity condition cannot be dropped: Lipschitz continuity in the parameters alone does not suffice. For linear softmax gating, the routing cost is of the same order as the gating term. Finally, for linear experts, we establish a matching minimax lower bound of order $Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}/n$, showing that the rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors.

2610.15111-d40c1f17d325.title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds
2610.15111-d40c1f17d325.abstract: Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of continuous-time dynamical systems provide rich structure for statistical learning. A central challenge is how to integrate data with PDE constraints in a principled way to improve generalization. In this paper, we characterize the statistical estimation and generalization properties of learning solutions to the heat equation with a noisy source function from finite, randomly sampled data. We first derive a novel variational formulation, which we characterize as the minimizer of loss function for an energy regularized and ellipticity debiased Sobolev regression. By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}---samples of the source function of the heat equation---to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.

2610.15281-222d2bd285c7.title: Imperfect Verifiers, Exact Targets: Inference-Time Scaling for Continuous Generation
2610.15281-222d2bd285c7.abstract: Verifier-guided inference-time scaling uses additional computation to score intermediate states and steer generation toward better outputs. However, imperfect intermediate verifiers can distort sampling, and repeated refinement alone does not ensure recovery of the desired reward-tilted distribution. We introduce Continuous-State Verifier-Guided Backtracking (CS-VGB), an inference-time scaling method for sampling from reward-tilted distributions with continuous generative models through repeated denoising and renoising. With correctly paired denoising and renoising transitions, the stationary distribution of CS-VGB at the clean checkpoint equals the desired reward-tilted target, even when intermediate verifiers are inaccurate.
